stances.claim: PNoy's Sona used the Maguindanao massacre as the centerpiece of his critique of predecessor's impunity -- making the case the centerpiece of his search for justice and the acid test of the criminal justice system

The November 23, 2009 'shooting, mangling and back-hoeing' of 58 defenseless civilians -- 32 of them media persons -- has been viewed by benefactors like Melinda de Jesus's Center for Media Freedom and Responsibility not only as criminal impunity but also as shameless assault on press freedom

After five years, the five consolidated murder cases originally filed against 197 accused -- 15 surnamed Ampatuan with Datu Andal 'Unsay' Ampatuan Jr. as main accused -- remain in the trial stage; the cases have received prime executive and judicial attention via venue transfer, dedicated judges, and SC-directed procedural innovations

The Judicial Affidavit Rule (no lengthy direct-examination Q&A, only cross-examination retained), partial-judgment authorization, and interlocutory-trial continuation have considerably sped up proceedings, but the cases are still far from resolved

Of 197 accused: 1 dropped, 1 turned state's witness, 1 dismissed, 4 deceased; the prosecution rested against 9 accused (Bong Andal, Saudi Mukamad, Talembo Masukat, Dexton Sapula, Abas Anongan, Kumini Inggo, Warden Legawan, Takpan Dilon, Mohammad Sangki) and expects to fully rest before year-end -- but defense will still present its side; no decision before PNoy's term ends June 30, 2016

During CJP's short stint as Chief Justice, he focused his judicial reform program on the 'Acid' problems that corrode justice: (1) Access to justice by the poor, (2) Corruption, (3) Incompetence of some judges, (4) Delay in delivery of quality justice -- PNoy has ineluctably made the Maguindanao massacre the acid test of all four

The criminal justice system was instituted under the 1987 Constitution to shield the innocent and underprivileged from the strong arm of the state that the Marcos dictatorship wrongly employed -- but ironically, these very rights are at times misused and abused to delay and frustrate the dispensation of justice; how to prevent this misuse and abuse is the other litmus challenge -- the long-term focus of judicial and prosecutorial reforms

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens his August 2, 2015 column -- the first in a three-column daang-matuwid series alongside A374 (three-senator PDAF) and A373 (GMA cases) -- with PNoy's Sona excerpt criticizing his predecessor's impunity: 'Every government official takes an oath to do right by our countrymen and to uphold the law. But it was clear: Our predecessor did precisely the opposite. We were all witnesses to the most appalling example, when 58 Filipinos were massacred in November 2009... The worst offense of all: their belief that they could get away with it, because they were in power.' (CJP notes the official English translation did not catch the exact lingual nuance of PNoy's original Filipino.) The opening reopened wounds in the long-winded trial of the November 23, 2009 'gory shooting, mangling and back-hoeing' of 58 defenseless civilians in Maguindanao -- six months before the 2010 presidential election, making the multiple murder a centerpiece of PNoy's search for justice. Many local and foreign benefactors -- like the Center for Media Freedom and Responsibility through Melinda de Jesus -- view this not only as a deadly example of criminal impunity but also as a shameless assault on press freedom, given 32 of the victims were media persons. Yet after five years, the five consolidated murder cases originally filed against 197 accused -- 15 of them surnamed Ampatuan, with Datu Andal 'Unsay' Ampatuan Jr. as main accused -- remain in the trial stage. The cases were given prime attention: venue moved from faraway Maguindanao to RTC Quezon City (better security and media focus, but logistical issues); Judge Jocelyn Solis-Reyes -- competent, with integrity and independence -- was relieved of all other cases and assigned two assisting judges; the SC directed implementation of the Judicial Affidavit Rule (no lengthy direct-examination Q&A; cross-examination retained), authorized partial judgments, and allowed continued trial despite pending interlocutory appeals. To date, of the 197 accused: 1 was dropped, 1 discharged as state's witness, 1 dismissed/virtually acquitted, 4 died (including clan patriarch Andal Ampatuan Sr.). 12 public prosecutors + 7 private prosecutors face 26 defense law firms; transcripts have thickened to 48 volumes and records to 101 'humongous' volumes; the court has heard 174 witnesses (93 prosecution, 23 defense, 58 private complainants) during continuous trials mostly at Camp Bagong Diwa in Taguig. Judge Solis-Reyes and her two assisting judges have disposed of 472 trial 'incidents' with only 22 remaining; they have resolved 59 bail petitions, with only Unsay Ampatuan's bail as the major one left. The court is now hearing the prosecution's evidence-in-chief simultaneously; the prosecution has rested against nine accused (Bong Andal, Saudi Mukamad, Talembo Masukat, Dexton Sapula, Abas Anongan, Kumini Inggo, Warden Legawan, Takpan Dilon, Mohammad Sangki) and expects to fully rest before year-end. But the many defense counsels will still present their sides -- CJP doubts any decision will be rendered before PNoy's term ends June 30, 2016. He closes with the 'Acid test': during his short stint as Chief Justice he focused his judicial reform program on the four 'Acid' problems that corrode justice -- (1) Access to justice by the poor, (2) Corruption, (3) Incompetence of some judges, (4) Delay in delivery of quality justice. From the start of his term up to his last Sona, PNoy has repeatedly alluded to the Maguindanao massacre as the grand example of his predecessor's impunity that he vowed to vindicate and eradicate -- ineluctably making the search for justice in Maguindanao the acid test of the criminal justice system. This system was instituted under the 1987 Constitution to shield the innocent and underprivileged from the strong arm of the state that the Marcos dictatorship wrongly employed to violate civil liberties and perpetuate itself. Ironically, however, these very rights are at times misused and abused to delay and frustrate the dispensation of justice. How to prevent this misuse and abuse is the other litmus challenge -- and in CJ's humble view, the long-term focus of judicial and prosecutorial reforms.
